Build A Cold and Flu Survival Kit To Get Your Baby Through Sick Season

Quick Summary

Experts recommend stocking your medicine cabinet with sick baby essentials like a thermometer, baby-safe chest rub, a fever reducer, and a nasal aspirator ahead of cold and flu season.

The first time my oldest son caught a cold was rough. He was barely four months old, and I was convinced his snotty nose was the start of something serious. I had a thermometer, but no batteries, and my “sick kit” basically amounted to a sample pack of Boogie Wipes from my baby shower.

A reassuring chat with our pediatrician helped ease my worries, but she kindly suggested that I stock up on some essentials for when (not if) this happened again, especially since we were in the thick of cold and flu season.

Fast forward more than a decade and two kids later, and I can honestly say the anxiety that hits when your baby’s congested never fully goes away (I still check to make sure my preteens are breathing at night when they’re stuffed up). However, I’ve learned that having the right tools on hand — beyond a prescription from the doctor! — makes all the difference. Consider this roundup your cold and flu survival kit: it includes all of the sick day essentials I’ve leaned on over the years to get my family through countless fevers, coughs, and late nights.

A Doctor’s Note

I spoke with Biljana Uzelac, M.D., a board-certified pediatrician with more than 20 years of experience and additional training in integrative medicine, about what families should know before stocking their medicine cabinet. Her top recommendations? Have a cool-mist humidifier, a nasal aspirator, and a saline spray ready to go.

She says most mild cold symptoms “can be managed at home with rest, fluids, and comfort measures.” For example, try dressing the baby in lightweight clothing, giving extra snuggles and skin-to-skin contact, and slightly elevating the crib mattress (by placing a rolled towel under it, never inside).

How I Chose What To Put in a Cold and Flu Kit

When putting together this survival kit, I leaned on three key factors:

Expert insights: I consulted pediatric advice from both the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and my interview with Dr. Uzelac, who walked me through what she recommends all families keep stocked at home.

Parent-tested picks: I pulled from my own trial and error after 13 cold and flu seasons, while also tapping into recommendations from the What to Expect Community to see what other parents swear by when their babies are sick.

Selection criteria: Everything included is safe for infants and approved by pediatricians, while also being easy to use and widely available (because when you need it, you can’t wait days for shipping).

In other words, these are the tools I wish I’d had on hand the first time my baby spiked a fever — and the ones I’ll never go without again.

Best Thermometer for Accurate Readings

Frida Baby Rectal Thermometer

Accurate digital readings

Quick to use

Backlit display

Can only be used rectally (not versatile for older kids)

Insertion tip length: 1.5 inches Power: CR2032 3V button cell battery

Why We Love It

When it comes to sick babies, accuracy is everything. This rectal thermometer was chosen as WTE’s best baby thermometer for precisely that reason. The AAP considers rectal thermometers the gold standard for infants, and FridaBaby’s version makes the process less intimidating.

The flexible tip and parent-friendly grip help you get a quick, accurate read in just 10 seconds. Plus, the backlit display means even middle-of-the-night checks are easy without turning on a light.

Best Saline Spray for Congested Babies

Little Remedies Spray and Drops

Safe for all ages

Dual design bottle (drop or spray)

Contains no alcohol

The bottle is relatively small

Quantity: 1 ounce

Why We Love It

Just like several WTE community parents, I preferred using Little Remedies Spray and Drops because it gave me the option of squeezing a couple of drops into a nostril instead of startling an already-fussy baby with a big spray up the nose. Either way you do it, this gentle saline spray moisturizes nasal passages and loosens mucus without any medication, so it’s perfect for even the tiniest babies. I always applied it before using the nasal aspirator to help get stubborn congestion moving, and it made a huge difference.

Best Nasal Aspirator for Stuffy Noses

Frida Baby NoseFrida SnotSucker

Dishwasher safe for easy cleaning

Powerful suction capability

No batteries required

Requires replacing filters over time

Recommended ages: Safe for infants and older babies

Why We Love It

You probably got a bulb syringe at the hospital when your baby was born, and while that works fine for clearing small amounts of snot, there’s truly no comparison to the suction power you get with theNoseFrida.

It tackles even the stuffiest noses using parent-generated suction (not as gross as it sounds — there’s a hygienic filter). With overwhelmingly positive feedback from parents and a tried-and-true design, it’s hands-down the best nasal aspirator for babies.

Best Humidifier (and Vaporizer and Night Light)

Vicks 3-in-1 SleepyTime Humidifier

No filter required

Runs up to 30 hours on one tank

Whisper-quiet operation

Water needs to be dumped each day

Dimensions: 8.15 x 8.6 x 8.23 inches

Capacity: 0.6 gallons

Why We Love It

The best baby humidifier is one that’s easy to clean and uses cool mist. A 2025 Sleep Awards winner, this 3-in-1 Vicks version (I bought it not too long ago to replace an old one, and it's an absolute workhorse!) checks all the boxes and then some.

It features a filterless design that’s simple to sanitize and a whisper-quiet motor that won’t wake your baby. It’s also a night light (cycle between seven different colors) and even provides cough and congestion relief as a vaporizer.

Best Chest Rub for Soothing

Zarabees Baby Soothing Chest Rub

Made with baby-safe natural ingredients

Free from parabens and petroleum

Lovely scent

Some babies may not tolerate scents well

Quantity: 1.5-ounce jar Recommended ages: 2 months+

Why We Love It

For little ones too young for medicated rubs, this gentle balm is a lifesaver. Made with eucalyptus, lavender, and beeswax, it helps soothe congestion without any potentially harsh ingredients.

It was a bedtime staple when my kids were congested — and it’s still part of our comfort ritual today because it smells incredible. Like several WTE community members, I’ve seen success applying this to my sons’ feet to help ease congestion.

Best Nose Wipes for Dry Mucus and Sensitive Skin

Boogie Wipes Saline Unscented Nose Wipes

Unscented and gentle on sensitive skin

Moisturizes with aloe and vitamin E

Easy to use on the go

Pricier than standard tissues

Quantity: 30 wipes per pack

Why We Love It

As mentioned above, Boogie Wipes were one of the few sick-baby essentials I actually had on hand the first time my oldest got sick — and I’m so grateful I did. Raw, chapped noses from dry tissues are no fun for babies (or parents).

These saline-infused wipes gently dissolve dried boogies without stinging or irritation. They’re perfect for clearing clogs before using an aspirator. I always reached for the unscented version since my little ones have sensitive skin — and they worked like a charm.

Best Ointment for Chapped Noses

Aquaphor Baby Healing Ointment

Multipurpose

Gentle enough for all ages

Dermatologist-recommended

Some parents don’t like how greasy it feels

Quantity: 7-ounce tube

Why We Love It

Aquaphoris one of those do-it-all staples every parent should have. From red noses to chapped cheeks, this ointment forms a protective barrier that helps irritated skin heal.

It’s especially great for preventing rashes from runny noses and frequent wiping. I kept the baby-specific version in nearly every room during cold and flu season — it’s that useful. And yes, I still use it for all sorts of things even now that my kids are older.

Best Pajamas To Dress A Sick Baby In

Little Sleepies Zippy

Machine washable

Made of soft bamboo that’s temperature-regulating

Fold-over mittens and feet

Pricey compared to other sleepers

Material: Bamboo Sizes: Preemie-3T

Why We Love It

When your baby is sick, comfort is everything. The Little Sleepies Zippy is a buttery-soft bamboo viscose sleeper that’s naturally temperature-regulating — perfect year-round, even when your little one is feverish.

It’s lightweight, machine washable, and built to last thanks to the stretchy flip-footed design that grows with your baby. Fold-over mittens help keep them from scratching at their stuffy nose, and the footies make it easy to try the chest-rub-on-feet trick without wrestling on socks.

Best Medicine Dispenser for Fussy Babies

Frida Baby MediFrida Accu-Dose Paci

Pacifier-style dispenser

Accurate dosing syringe included

Works with liquid medications

Some parents say cleaning it properly is tedious

Material: BPA-free silicone

Why We Love It

If your doctor prescribes medication — or you’re giving a baby-safe OTC pain reliever (Infants' Tylenol is a resounding favorite!) — getting it down can feel like an Olympic event. The MediFrida Accu-Dose Paci makes it easier by delivering medicine through a pacifier design that bypasses taste buds and reduces spit-up.

When parents in the WTE community asked for medicine-giving hacks, this gadget came up more than any other. It wasn’t around when my boys were babies, but I really wish it had been.

Best Cold and Cough Remedy

Boiron Baby ColdCalm

Mess-free single-dose vials

No artificial ingredients or dyes

Non-drowsy formula

Not all parents feel homeopathy works

Quantity: 30 doses Dosage: 1 pre-measured dose.

Recommended ages: 6 months and up

Why We Love It

Many parents instinctively reach for OTC cold and cough medicines, but Dr. Uzelac notes that “most are not recommended for children under 6.” Instead, she often turns to gentler measures — often homeopathy.

“Homeopathy has a low risk of side effects and won’t mask symptoms, so it can be a great place to start,” she says. She recommends ColdCalm Baby for nasal congestion because it’s suitable for little ones as young as 6 months. These single-dose liquid vials target common cold symptoms like runny noses and congestion, and parents in the WTE Community swear by them during sick season.

Cold and Flu Kit FAQs

What can I give my baby if they have a fever?

Always check with your doctor before giving your baby any fever-reducing medication. The AAP says infant acetaminophen can help reduce a fever (WTE parents prefer Infants' Tylenol), and ibuprofen may be used for babies over 6 months. You can also apply a cool compress or give a lukewarm bath to help bring their temperature down.

Are there any essential oils that are good for a sick baby?

Check with your pediatrician first. Using essential oils directly on babies under 2 is generally not recommended — their skin and airways are too sensitive, and oils can cause irritation or breathing issues if misused. However, some baby-safe products (like the chest rub above) use diluted essential oils to aid congestion or sleep.

When should I call a doctor?

Most colds clear up within 7 to 10 days, according to Dr. Uzelac, but you should call your pediatrician if your baby has a fever that lasts longer than three days, a fever above 102°F in older infants and children, or any signs of dehydration (fewer wet diapers, dark urine, no tears when crying).

For babies under 2 months, any temperature of 100.4°F or higher is an emergency and requires an ER visit. Other red flags include trouble breathing, wheezing, persistent ear or sinus pain, bluish lips or face, seizures, or behavior that feels “off.”

“You know your child best,” Dr. Uzelac adds, “so if something is out of the ordinary, seek help.”
